items.title: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?
items.summary_original: This article is a sponsored by Level Access Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report . Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up. We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most said they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage. items.title: ukrainian artists reimagine historic tree of life mosaic with 5,000 reclaimed fragments
items.summary_original: UKRAINIAN ARTISTS BRING TREE OF LIFE TO COP31 A historic Ukrainian mosaic is finding a new life at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, where thousands of reclaimed fragments come together in an interactive installation celebrating art, memory, and collective creativity. Titled Tree of Life, the project reimagines a celebrated 1967 artwork from Mariupol through a contemporary composition made from approximately 5,000 pieces of glass, ceramics, tiles, and recovered construction materials. Initiated by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Ukraine, the installation was developed by artists from the Monument-ta mosaic studio and the Alla Horska and Viktor Zaretskyi Foundation, with financial support from the Government of Japan. items.title: john pawson sets white ribbon staircase against 18th century baroque portal at the madrid EDITION
items.summary_original: THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE MADRID EDITION John Pawson takes his cue at The Madrid EDITION hotel from an eighteenth-century baroque portal he inherited. Spanish architect Pedro de Ribera carved it for the chapel of the Monte de Piedad, the charitable pawnshop that Francisco Piquer, chaplain of the Descalzas Reales convent across the square, founded in 1702 to lend to the poor. The savings bank that grew out of that pawnshop demolished the chapel in the 1960s and kept the portal, resetting it on the face of its new office building. Sheep, wooden toys, polka dots and foam – these are just a few of the things that French illustrator Ines Launay keeps close at hand when she's making work, alongside a fondness for wandering, textile crafts, costumes and the occasional absurdity. It's a wonderfully peculiar collection of interests, but one that makes perfect sense when you look through her portfolio, where loose pencil marks, wonky characters, and little snippets of everyday life come together in playful, unexpected ways. items.title: Studio Kiln builds a shape-shifting character for weight loss app Reset
items.summary_original: Meet Ester, who's made of tumbling blocks and sits at the heart of a warmer, less preachy identity. Sadly, the terms 'weight-loss app' and 'empathy' don't naturally go together. Typically, such apps feel more like a nagging aunt: counting every calorie, logging every slip, basically doing everything but calling you an overweight loser. Reset wants to do things differently. First launched in 2019, this app is aimed at those who'd rather not count every calorie and want to progress at their own pace. It begins by calculating your metabolic type, then adapts its guidance accordingly. To better convey that approach, Reset turned to Studio Kiln, the design studio founded in Falmouth and now splitting its time between Cornwall and London, as we explored in this interview a couple of months back.

items.title: rune bosse puts living trees on life support in a vision of ecological collapse
items.summary_original: rune bosse's lung trees imagine a forest on life support Danish artist Rune Bosse places living trees on artificial life support in Lung Trees, an installation presented at the Danish Architecture Center in Copenhagen as part of its Age of Nature exhibition, which ran through September 2026. Each tree stands inside a transparent, inflated plastic enclosure, and is surrounded by mechanical equipment and artificial lighting. With their branches reaching toward overhead lamps, each tree seems to have been removed from the forest and placed under intensive care. The installation imagines a future in which trees might depend on technology to survive, even as humans continue to depend on the ecological systems that trees help sustain. It reverses a relationship we tend to take for granted. Fores

Jeder Baum steht in einem transparenten, aufgeblasenen Kunststoffgehäuse und ist von mechanischer Ausrüstung und künstlicher Beleuchtung umgeben. Da ihre Äste bis zu den Deckenlampen reichen, scheint es, als ob jeder Baum aus dem Wald entfernt und auf die Intensivstation gebracht worden wäre. Es kehrt eine Beziehung um, die wir normalerweise für selbstverständlich halten. Fores

Creative makers and builders have always learned their medium by working with it, from grinding pigments to HTML. Models are the next material, and you need to learn them by building. items.summary_original: WHEN ARCHITECTURE LEARNS TO LISTEN Speaking with Arnaud Behzadi is something of a masterclass in understanding architecture beyond aesthetics. For the Paris-based architect, spaces are living entities, capable of provoking emotions, awakening memories, and shaping human relationships, provided they have been designed with enough sensitivity. His approach challenges the notion that beauty is something we merely observe. Instead, he believes it is something we experience, often without fully understanding why. This conviction runs through his work, from his furniture collection BAM to two of his latest hospitality projects: the reinvention of Doobie’s, an iconic Parisian restaurant , and Pavyllon Lyon, conceived in collaboration with celebrated chef Yannick Alléno. items.title: bacteria become the builders in ETH zurich’s exploration of living architecture
items.summary_original: what if bacteria could build the architecture of the future? At ETH Zurich , researcher Karen Antorveza Paez explores the possibility of bacteria becoming architectural collaborators by combining microorganisms , sand and digital manufacturing to produce solid building elements. Through a process known as biocementation, bacteria bind loose grains together with calcium carbonate, the mineral found in limestone, mussel shells, and chalk. items.title_de: Bakterien werden zu Baumeistern bei der Erforschung lebendiger Architektur an der ETH Zürich
items.summary_de: Was wäre, wenn Bakterien die Architektur der Zukunft bauen könnten? An der ETH Zürich erforscht die Forscherin Karen Antorveza Paez die Möglichkeit, dass Bakterien zu architektonischen Kollaborateuren werden, indem sie Mikroorganismen, Sand und digitale Fertigung kombinieren, um solide Bauelemente herzustellen. Durch einen Prozess namens Biozementierung binden Bakterien lose Körner mit Kalziumkarbonat, dem Mineral, das in Kalkstein, Muschelschalen und Kreide vorkommt. Durch die Integration dieses biologischen Prozesses mit 3D-Druck und Roboterfertigung untersucht ihre Forschung, wie Mikroorganismen an der Gestaltung der gebauten Umwelt teilnehmen können, und stellt damit die Vorstellung von Architektur als einer ausschließlich von Menschen geschaffenen Praxis in Frage. Die Forschung führt ein alternatives Verständnis der Konstruktion ein, bei dem Mikroorganismen aktiv sind

items.summary_original: PARAMETRIC FONTS I’m going to talk about a future. Not the future: I’ve abandoned any pretension of prediction; AI makes the landscape too unstable for that. It’s simply a plausible scenario. One in which AI doesn’t replace the type designer, but amplifies their operational capacity through supercharged workflows. In that future, the structural constraints that today limit huge multilingual or multiaxis “superprojects” disappear. Families can be produced across multiple writing systems, including those traditionally foreign to many Western designers, like Arabic or CJK, without requiring an unmanageable multiplication of resources. items.title: The AI mind tax that afflicts those who use AI best
items.summary_original: One person, a dozen tools, and nothing connecting them but her. AI was supposed to make work easier, but for the people who use it most, it just became a different kind of work, and a whole lot of exhaustion. The promise of the tech was that AI would make work easier, and, sure, in plenty of ways it came true, but for the people using it the hardest, it created a second job nobody considered, managing the pile of tools that now does the work for you. The folks who stay sharp hold onto what the machine still can’t do for them, their judgment, their ability to work with other people, and some grip on where the work actually stands, but there’s a price to pay for that. items.title: Why are we cloning Photoshop?
items.summary_original: AI is making it easy to recreate professional tools. I suspect there’s a bigger opportunity being overlooked. Editing in PhotoCraft October saw the release of PhotoCraft , an open-source Photoshop clone built with AI that had a similar capability set, but without Adobe Creative Cloud’s exorbitant monthly price tag. Building software with AI has become so cheap that a complex product which would have typically taken a large team to develop, can now be spun up for a fraction of the cost by a lone developer and a band of AI agents. items.title: Every click has a price now. Who designs how that “feels”?
items.summary_original: As the all-you-can-eat AI era is ending, UX designers must adapt to a new reality Since the democratization of AI, roughly by the end of 2022, companies sold access to their products for less than it costs them to run. That didn’t last long. Now, to try the latest models or pro versions of certain tools, users need to pay extra in tokens, which have unofficially become AI’s currency. More and more products are moving to credit- and usage-based pricing, meaning every action comes with a cost. So how does that price show up on screen?
